item.title: Chinese Firms Exit Kenya Rare Earths Race as U.S. Companies Move In
item.description: By Ammu Kannampilly Engineering giant Fluor Corp is among a group of mostly U.S. investors vying to develop Kenya’s Mrima Hill critical minerals deposit, after two Chinese companies pulled out of the process, Kenya’s mining minister told Reuters on Friday. A final …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
By Ammu Kannampilly

Engineering giant Fluor Corp is among a group of mostly U.S. investors vying to develop Kenya’s Mrima Hill critical minerals deposit, after two Chinese companies pulled out of the process, Kenya’s mining minister told Reuters on Friday.

A final decision would be announced within three weeks, he said.

Reuters is first to report Fluor Corp’s bid, the timing of the final announcement and the withdrawal of the Chinese companies — Hunan Research Institute for Nonferrous Metals and Jinan Yuxiao Group Co. Ltd.

U.S. President Donald Trump has made securing access to critical minerals a priority of his administration, inking deals with a number of African nations as Washington looks to cut dependence on top producer China, which dominates the global supply chain and has tightened export controls in recent years.

China is also a dominant player in Africa’s mining industry.

Kenya’s mining minister Hassan Ali Joho said that five contenders had submitted tenders on October 21 for the Mrima Hill deposit in southern Kenya, around 65 kilometers from the port city of Mombasa. They include two U.S. consortia, one U..S-affiliated consortium, an Australian consortium and a Kenyan-British joint venture.

“American entities have strongly showcased or demonstrated interest by participating in our transparent process in identifying the developer of Mrima Hill,” Joho said in an interview.

“Within the next two to three weeks we should be able to award Mrima Hills to the successful bidder.”

Joho said preliminary indicators suggest the coastal deposit contains tens of billions of dollars’ worth of rare earth minerals and niobium, a metal used in aerospace manufacturing, with deposits primarily mined in Brazil and Canada.

Chinese Firms Said to Have Submitted Other Bids

The two U.S. consortia are Meridian Mineral Holdings, which includes Fluor Corp and Tetra Tech, and Frontier Minerals LLC, which includes rare earths startup ReElement Technologies. Joho also said a U.S.-affiliated consortium called Mrima Earth was on the shortlist, led by Critical Metals Corp, which is pursuing the Tanbreez rare earth project in Greenland.

A Kenyan-British joint venture called Gem of Dreams also submitted a tender, as has Australia’s RareX in a tie-up with Iluka Resources. Rare X announced in July that it had been shortlisted to compete for the project.

Fluor Corp previously built the Eneabba rare earths refinery in Western Australia for Iluka Resources, but the two are now aggressively competing for the Mrima Hill project.

A representative for the Australian joint venture told Reuters that Fluor Corp was not licensed to use any intellectual property related to the Eneabba plant.

“Should Fluor make use of or appear to be making use of Iluka’s IP in designing and constructing a processing plant for Mrima Hill, there would be a high chance of legal action to protect IP rights,” the representative said.

Fluor Corp and Meridian did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on the Australian consortium’s comment.

‘No Pressure’ From Washington or Beijing

The other three consortia and the Chinese companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Mrima Hill project.

Joho said he did not know why the Chinese firms withdrew, adding that the Kenyan government did not directly engage with the bidders.

“We haven’t had any conversation with anybody, and we haven’t offered any alternative to anybody… We want a transparent process,” he said.

Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters that the Chinese firms had bid for other state mining projects in Kenya on the same day that the Mrima Hill tender was due last week. It was not immediately clear which projects received bids, but both sources said four other tenders for coltan, manganese, copper and chromite projects were due that day.

Joho told Reuters that one of the Chinese companies did file a bid for another project the same day, but declined to elaborate, saying it would compromise the process.

He said Kenya had faced “no pressure” from either Beijing or Washington on the issue.

“I don’t think it is in the place of anybody to tell us how and with whom to work. Our decisions are purely informed by the interests of this country.”

Shift to Domestic Processing

African nations have pushed in recent years to process more of the minerals they produce domestically, marking a shift toward keeping more value on the continent.

Kenya’s President William Ruto told Reuters in June that his government was close to signing a critical minerals deal with the United States, under which Nairobi would process its own resources domestically.

Officials in the Trump administration have also said the U.S. intends to help Kenya develop a critical minerals processing industry.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson told Reuters that U.S. companies had proven track records and a commitment to local processing.

“The U.S. Government will take every opportunity to help American businesses invest in emerging sectors and developing economies, including the mining sector,” the spokesperson said.

Ruto has previously said that Kenya would not choose between Washington and Beijing, but instead pursue multiple partnerships aligned with its own economic priorities.

In addition to rare earths and niobium, Kenya is also believed to have large untapped deposits of lithium, graphite, copper and nickel.

item.title: China’s New Tunnel-Boring Export Controls Cast Shadow Over Warming Ties With India
item.description: Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface. China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized …
item.dc:creator: Rudy Lu
item.content:encoded:
Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface.

China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized construction equipment last week, a move Chinese analysts have interpreted as an attempt to restrict India’s strategic infrastructure development, particularly along the countries’ disputed Himalayan border.

The regulations, issued jointly by the Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs , cover tunnel-boring machines (TBMs), including shield machines and hard-rock tunnel borers, as well as critical components such as cutterheads, main drive systems and remanufacturing technologies. They also extend to specialized walking excavators capable of operating in difficult terrain and concrete-spraying machines used to reinforce tunnels at high altitudes.

The equipment is widely used in civilian infrastructure projects, such as metro systems, high-speed railways, highways, and hydropower facilities. The same machines can also be used to build military transport corridors, strategic tunnels, and other infrastructure supporting troop and equipment movements in mountainous border regions.

Set to take effect on November 18, the rules establish a two-tier export approval system.

Exporters shipping covered equipment to what Beijing describes as “sensitive countries and regions that have disputes with China” must obtain government licenses. Shipments to other destinations are subject to a simpler registration process.

Overseas organizations and individuals are prohibited from transferring or supplying Chinese-origin controlled equipment to sensitive destinations without Beijing’s approval, potentially affecting international contractors that purchase machinery in one country and redeploy it elsewhere.

Beijing has not publicly identified which countries fall under the sensitive-destination category.

The announcement has raised concerns in India, where major infrastructure projects remain dependent on imported tunneling equipment. According to a 2020 investigation by The Indian Express , industry suppliers estimated that nearly 90 percent of tunnel-boring machines deployed across India had links to China..

India’s Economic Times reported that government officials plan to consult industry stakeholders to mitigate the potential impact . While officials played down the likelihood of widespread delays to highway construction, they acknowledged that shortages of specialized machinery could affect major projects, such as the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed railway, India’s first under-construction high-speed bullet train project.

New Delhi has already begun efforts to reduce its dependence on imported equipment.

Reuters reported in August that India was preparing a $1.2 billion manufacturing incentive program aimed at attracting $1.8 billion in investment over seven years. Tunnel-boring machines are among the priority products.

Li Guangman, a senior researcher at the Kunlunce Research Institute, a leftist, pro-government Chinese think tank, said that restricting tunnel-boring equipment would allow Beijing to constrain India’s construction of military transport networks near the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border separating Indian-controlled territory from Chinese-controlled territory.

Bloomberg reported in August that India is planning to invest $4.7 billion in railway upgrades along its borders with China, Pakistan and Bangladesh over the next two years. Li argued that advanced tunneling machinery could help India build all-weather transport corridors through the Himalayas, allowing troops and military supplies to move more easily across the mountainous frontier.

The restrictions also come amid renewed territorial friction. India’s Home Ministry announced early this month standardized names for 28 locations and geographical features in Ladakh, including areas disputed with China.

China’s Foreign Ministry firmly opposed the announcement , reiterating that Beijing has never recognized the “so-called Union Territory of Ladakh,” which India had established “unilaterally and illegally.”
